One of my favourite games. I already played it outside of steam, and bought it here again to support the developer. Decent story, interesting world, lots of gameplay and very varied scenes. Shimobashira Workshop already released a few good games before this one, Ambrosia especially, and Enishia afterwards, which are both good games as well. But my favourite is still Celesphonia just because it feels like it has the most content, longer story, and overall more rounded gameplay. I also personally prefer the magical girl theme over the nun style in the other game but they are still good games. Patch is absolutely recommended, without it the world wouldn't feel as 'realistic'. Be nice to Amane, as some of the dark scenes can be really dark on a loss, but just don't lose and there is also a lot of consensual content. :)

Gameplay is the typical RPGMaker style, but you can pick and choose your actual fight style. Can be melee, any elemental magic like fire/ice/electric/dark etc, there are utility buff or debuff spells, you can upgrade your equipment in different ways like glass cannon build, tank build with regen, or even a seduction build. 

Difficulty can be selected and has a rather strong impact on the gameplay, on the easier difficulties you can mostly chill, on the harder ones you actually have to plan your build, prepare utility and healing items, have an upgrade path etc. Even the items can be either bought, built with monster parts, or other special parts.  This also makes for fun replayvalue and just going a different fight style. One thing I also really enjoy, you can activate auto defeat of weaker opponents if your character is a lot stronger in comparison, making revisitting older areas for some missed materials a lot nicer. 

If you somehow get a gameover, there is usually a way to automatically get reset to the last part before the gameover to then prevent it, but gameovers are rare and usually Amane just has some....experience and then somehow escapes. Her personality is also affected by these experiences, though you can still say no to certain 'level ups' in that regard, but a lot of the content is gated behind her becoming more experienced or more corrupted. Corruption is a different kind of magical thing. There is also a 'domination' level of the enemy over the city, this could technically be seen as a time limit, but it's very easy to reduce with ingame items, upgrades, or just doing a mission. Once you've completed the main quest it also disappears, and then you still have more after content. Lots of funny references and memes included as well, so it's entertaining throughout. I hope the developers make a sequel or similar style.

Magical Girl Celesphonia is a vibrant and fast-paced bullet-hell shoot ’em up that combines classic arcade-style action with the charm and flair of magical girl anime aesthetics. Developed by TRIAVNIA GAMES, it stands out in a crowded genre by blending intense, skill-based gameplay with a colorful narrative and visually striking presentation. The game offers an experience that will appeal to both hardcore shmup veterans looking for a challenging run and newcomers intrigued by its approachable mechanics and whimsical style.

From the moment you start, Magical Girl Celesphonia immerses you in a vivid world full of bright, dynamic sprites and beautifully animated characters. The visual design heavily leans on magical girl tropes—sparkling effects, elaborate costumes, and a pastel color palette—that contrast intriguingly with the high-octane bullet patterns filling the screen. Each level is packed with detailed backgrounds and inventive enemy designs that keep the player engaged beyond just dodging a hailstorm of bullets. The boss battles deserve special mention, offering large, multi-phase encounters that combine pattern memorization with quick reflexes, punctuated by spectacular visual and sound effects that heighten the intensity.

Gameplay revolves around navigating complex bullet patterns while delivering powerful counterattacks using Celesphonia’s unique magical abilities. Unlike some traditional shmups that rely heavily on memorization and precision alone, this game introduces a resource management aspect tied to the magical girl’s powers. Players must decide when to unleash devastating special attacks or conserve energy for survival, adding a strategic layer to the fast reflexes required. The controls are tight and responsive, ensuring that every dodge and shot feels deliberate and satisfying. Additionally, the game incorporates a scoring system rewarding risk-taking and skillful play, providing replayability for those aiming to climb leaderboards or perfect their runs.

Narratively, Magical Girl Celesphonia embraces its anime inspiration with a light but engaging story that unfolds between levels through charming dialogue and cutscenes. The plot, while not overly complex, gives context to the protagonist’s journey and her battles against various magical adversaries threatening her world. This narrative thread adds emotional weight and personality to the gameplay, making the battles feel meaningful rather than just abstract challenges. The characters, especially Celesphonia herself, are designed with care, showcasing distinctive personalities and expressions that further enhance the game’s overall appeal.

The game offers multiple difficulty settings, catering to a broad range of skill levels. Casual players can enjoy the spectacle and story without being overwhelmed, while the harder modes provide a brutal test of precision and endurance for shmup enthusiasts. This scalability ensures that Magical Girl Celesphonia remains accessible while still challenging those seeking to master its mechanics. There is also a robust progression system, with upgrades and power-ups that can be unlocked to customize playstyle and increase survivability, encouraging experimentation with different strategies and abilities.

While Magical Girl Celesphonia excels in many areas, it does have a few minor drawbacks. Some players might find that the bullet patterns, while varied, occasionally lack the complexity and unpredictability seen in top-tier bullet-hell titles. The story, though charming, is relatively brief and might leave players wanting more depth or character development. An H-game with some serious production value for it... for the usual standards. The world is sizable and fun to explore, the dungeons actually have obstacles, can become easier if you stealth around, and there are plenty of 'builds' to try to use on your heroine, maybe even an excessive amount due to all the unlockables compared on how many you can equip at once.

Lastly, it is also challenging if you want it to be. There is an extra difficulty to use, and several mechanics that can lead to an irrecoverable game over that may make you have to start over if you screw up a little too much. TLDR at the bottom

[h1] Good [/h1]
- As an RPG, there is a lot of world exploration you can do. Tour around the school to find these "medals" that you can trade for stuff. Many shops to explore to find gear and the vending machines are all functional (even in combat stages). Activities to do and H scenes to unlock here and there. NPC dialogues even change depending on your condition (ex. wearing provocative clothing). It really was a blast to explore the world.
- The protagonist has an actual personality (not a self insert). And unlike most corruption games, the personality is not just "pure innocent girl". This protagonist does know about lewd things, they just aren't used to them.
- The corruption aspect is executed pretty well, at least in my opinion. Initially, some scenes and activities are locked. You have to increase your "lust" stat to unlock them. At first you increase it by getting groped and other light stuff. Then you unlock heavier things like prostitution.
- The amount of H things in this game is simply expansive. Bathhouse, streaming, exhibitionism, glory hole, tentacles, bukkake, and so on. Lots of clothes and costumes, and you can even make them see-through with an item. There are these "titles" that work like achievements for doing lots of a H activity, and they passively change your stats like "shame resistance increased"
- While the combat system is mediocre (explained below), there are ways to auto resolve combat so you don't have to sit through every single battle. This is a feature that the dev's previous game Ambrosia did not (and is one of the main weaknesses of that game imo)
- The structure of the RPG progression and world exploration is just right in my opinion. It is not too restricted that you feel there is only 1 thing you can do at any given moment ("go to the next dungeon" or "go to this part of town"). It is also not too loose that you feel lost on what you're supposed to do next (Ambrosia was like this).
- Soundtrack isn't groundbreaking but it's not bad and works well as a support for the game's overall atmostphere. A reocurring instrument is the saxophone, and I think it works well for the game's "modern day" setting, compared to traditional instruments like the violin.
- Story is also not particularly special, but it's ok enough for a passing grade. The villains and plot are cartoonish, but it fits with the overall magical girl theme, which would normally be a genre for children (if it didn't have H in it).
- Yes, there is a way to unlock all scenes after you beat the final boss. You don't have to intentionally lose.
- Amount of content is just right. The point you start getting bored is also around the game's end.
- Can be played one handed
- The game was probably intended to be played with the only the keyboard, but mouse controls still work if you don't like the keyboard.

[h1] Major Complaints [/h1]
- The combat isn't particularly unique or tactical. The abilities are pretty basic and shallow, they have little tactical depth. Most of the combat strategy in this game is simply making a coherent build.
- Because of the previous point, high difficulties aren't that fun in this game. Even moreso in the early game, as you don't yet have access to the powerful skills (no heal, no elemental weaknesses, no buffs). High difficulty simply adds more health and damage to the enemies, and there's nothing you can do about that other than grind levels. Chapter 1 is the worst point for this. At easy and normal difficulties, you can get to the boss and win in 1 run. At higher difficulties, you will have to grind the enemies more to level up enough to be able to win the boss.
- The clothing tearing feature feels half baked. The outfit only visually changes at 50% and 0% durability (I would've liked more breakpoints). The 50% visual also has barely any damage on it. The 0% visual is lazy: it's left right asymmetrical, but the sprites in and out of combat clearly had a horizontal mirror applied at some point. I mean, out of combat has more holes on the outfit's right side, but in combat has more holes int he left side. 0% also still has lots of fabric left despite being, you know, 0 percent durability.
- The H aspects of combat also feel half baked. Binding stuns you from combat, but all you need to do is hold down X or esc to get out of it. In practice, unless you're intentionally letting yourself be molested, this feature is more of an annoyance than a combat mechanic. And when you do get molested, arousal, pleasure, and climax seem to do absolutely nothing in combat. Why do the enemies even bother with H attacks?

[h1] Minor Complaints [/h1]
- You have to get a patch from the Kagura Games website. Thankfully, it's very easy (the instructions they give are literally 3 steps)
- There isn't a quick visual indicator on who's currently talking in a dialogue. Other games might make the non talkers' sprites darker like it's "in the background". Here you have to read the name on the dialogue box. For most conversations you can still easily tell who's talking by context (ex. if it sounds evil it's probably the enemy), but in some situations you have no choice but to read the name every time (ex. at the start of the game when you don't know the characters' personalities yet)
- No chat log for when you accidentally press next dialog
- Some equipment don't tell you what they do. Armour choices might say "balanced type" but they don't easily show how much stats increase. There are also things with a description and that's it; equipping it doesn't seem to result in any stat changes, so we're just left confused what it does. I still do not know what the "Another Soul" equip does; it doesn't seem to have anything to do with souls.
- Lack of H scenes with characters other than the protagonist. There are 2 other characters, but they have few scenes and are both flat chested. Also one of them isn't even voiced.
- Reflective bulwark has too low a trigger chance at lower tiers. It finally gets good at RB 4, but at that point you're near the final boss so you won't get much use out of it (In fact, realistically to get the materials you have to run through the final dungeon multiple times, so it's pointless by the time you craft it). And the post final boss content cannot be bulwarked, which is pretty annoying.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
I have played a good number of H games on Steam. Magical Girl Celesphonia is possibly the best one I've played so far. Its main strength is its RPG world exploration and interaction, with lots of activities to do.
The game isn't perfect. Its main flaw is its mediocre combat (though mitigated by auto resolve). But most everything else is done right, occupying the sweet spot of too little and too much. Packed with a lot of content, this game is very much worth the money, and it goes on sale often, too.

Classic 2D JRPG experience with patchable H contents. Very well worth the time.

[Story]
Standard magical girl trope but cleverly merged with H elements. Compared to other straightforward H games, this game actually tells a complete story that is enjoyable in itself. I think this world building really elevates the whole H part of the game by offering you the moral choice, rather than just mindlessly going after lewdness. 

[Graphics]
Classic 2D experience with beautiful scenery. The game is presented with a huge collection of beautiful 2D illustrations to keep the player engaged. While there is very little animation and almost all illustrations are static, the game does find its way to provoke your imaginations.

[Voice acting]
While there is no voiced lines at all in this game, the "ambient" voice acting during H scenes are insanely well done. The audio loops change seamlessly as you progress through a scene. It's done so well that I never realize there is a loop anywhere. The voices are so lewd that it makes up for the lack of animations.

[Combat]
Standard turn-based JRPG with H elements. I'm quite satisfied with the right amount of depth with the combat system - while being quite straightforward, the game offers a wide variety of skills and gear options you can mess around. It didn't take me too much effort to find an OP build to have fun. The H elements do not play a role in determining winning or losing a battle and it's completely up to your own moral standard whether to fight the corruption or not - which is the main charm of the game.

[Difficulty]
The difficulty is average compared to other JRPG titles - which is a good thing for this game since a lot of the fun comes from the H interactions rather than the difficulty challenge itself. I started the game on Hard difficulty and switched to Very Hard halfway through. In Very Hard, you get in-game trophy items by beating the bosses but otherwise there is no extra awards. I'd say cranking up the difficulty on your first playthrough actually enhances your experience because a lot of H scenes involve losing battles and there is no punishment otherwise. Compared to typical JRPGs, this game is surprisingly not grindy at all, and all progression is very well paced. Took me around 37 hrs to finish all main contents and maxing out in the first playthrough and I'll definitely come back to finish the remaining collectibles.

[Music]
The music is surprisingly well done. Not only individual tracks are pleasing to the ear, the game offers a generous variety of music loops so that I never find myself bored while chilling in the game world. In a lot of games the music can be too repetitive to the point that I'd have to turn off the music before I go insane, but it's certainly not the case here.

Overall I highly recommend this game for its overall experience combining classic JRPG gameplay and peak H materials.

One of the better RPGMaker Prostitution Sims available, with decent polish, that doesn't manage to elevate the game above the shortcomings of the genre.

Uncensor patch available from the developer's website, although it does require e-mail registration and login to access.

I completed the game in 16 hours, but the vast majority of that was grinding through very repetitive RPGMaker combat.  The progression system, combined with a significant NG+ mode, could add a substantial amount of time to that; but sitting through that much dull RPGMaker combat strikes me as more masochistic than the game's heroine.

[h1]The game focuses heavily on RPGMaker combat[/h1]

It's polished, and one of the better examples of the medium; but it's still repetitive and tedious busywork that doesn't belong in an H-game.  Yeah it's nice the skills are incorporated into a novel progression system, etc – but it doesn't make the grinding any less of a chore.

Having the heroine be a Magical Girl somewhat makes the combat slightly more creative than the typical "generic JRPG fantasy" crud you get from the genre's default setting; but it's really the bare minimum you should expect from a retail product.

[h1]The game runs into all of the pitfalls of the medium, and doesn't offer any substantial solutions[/h1]

Same ludonarrative disconnect between RPGMaker combat and erotic storytelling; same ludonarrative dissonance of controlling a female character, requiring you to "throw fights to see H-scenes" and deliberately walk her into moral hazards.

As with most games in this genre, it fumbles its core theme (moral corruption) by making all of the narrative entirely disposable and redundant - choosing, as is typical, to abstract out lust and moral degradation to a lewdness bar.
It's got unlockable titles, as is familiar in titles such as [i]Ideology in Friction[/i] or [i]Kamekaze Komittee Ouka 2[/i]; and like in those games they totally fail to have any narrative impact whatsoever.  Compare that to [i]Karryn's Prison[/i], where the unlocking of passives actually creates a narrative within the sandbox - something its imitators all fail at.
All the hallmarks of a game that's throwing H-content into the mix without any thought into what its purpose is other than to go "look, there's tiddies!  Ain't this just like an eroge?!"

The goal of games like this should be to give characters interesting tasks to perform around town; the decisions involved with which have specific consequences and thus drive a player-engineered story.  Thus establisingh narrative stakes - both for the characters, their relationships, but most importantly for the erotic themeing and experience as a whole.

Instead so many releases regard H-scenes as mere porn to throw in the faces of players at arbitrary points in the game as a tick-box content inclusion exercise; which ends up making them both unsexy and without value.  This game is no exception.

[h1]The setting is a good one, and decently presented.  But the game is more interested in sending you through boring dungeons than actually telling a worthwhile story within the setting.[/h1]

The city has different zones to explore, with different sections and unique events.  It's a bit reminiscent of [i]Fleeting Iris[/i] in how promising the locales are.

But, like most comparable H-games, you quickly realise how superficial this element is.  [i]Fleeting Iris[/i] and [i]Scars of Summer[/i] suffer from being too linear and locking you into strict, but brief, linear Visual Novel routes.
Conversely games like [i]Country Girl Keiko[/i]; [i]President Yukino[/i]; [i]Kamekaze Komitee Ouka 2[/i]; etc, etc treat locations in the town as arbitrary lone triggers for disconnected disposable H-scenes which fail at basic story-telling.

The superior presentation in this game makes a token gesture at reaching for a decent middle ground between the two; but totally fails to find something valuable in that space.

Instead of embarking on a cam-girl career leading to a dramatic tension between your school, home, and superhero identities - it's just a random side-job that has some H-scenes associated with it.
Exploring a growing kink in exhibitionism could lead to an emotional reckoning, which shapes how other characters interact with the protagonist, and how she responds to them.  Instead it's just, you guessed it, a trigger for a handful of disposable forgettable generic H-scenes.
Getting a job promoting a sex-shop in a seedy part of town could leave the main character exposed and vulnerable in a dangerous situation, where the pressures of having a hospitalised father meet the hard end of consumerist sexualisation.  But nope, just another nothing burger to be discarded.

[h1]The game is allergic to telling any story except for a bland two-dimensional insipid RPGMaker adventure[/h1]

As is typical, you get the sense that the characters suffer spontaneous amnesia whenever h-events are resolved, carrying on like nothing has happened. 
Which means it's not particularly sexy.  It's just conveyor-belt fet content that is better consumed for free from hentai websites.

The fact that this game is far more polished than the majority of its competitors doesn't detract from how unambitious its fundamental design is.  You've seen it before with the game's predecessor [i]Ambrosia[/i]; and this game doesn't really offer much more.

[h1]If all you want is a neat and tidy JRPG with some decent quality hentai art, it's fine.  You'll enjoy it.[/h1]

It's pretty much on a par with [i]Meltys Quest[/i] in pretty much every single sense; so if you want more of the same of that, you're in luck.

If, instead, you're looking at the positive feedback and are expecting this to be some sort of revolutionary or next-level product, you're going to be disappointed.
